column4: Woe that day to the deniers announces the class whom 83:11 identifies specifically as denying the Day of Recompense.
Only a transgressing sinner denies that day, identifying moral trespass as the posture behind refusal of the final account.
The question “What brought you into Saqar?” opens the itemized audit answered by neglected prayer, failure to feed the poor, and denial in 74:43-46.
The arrival of certainty closes the period in which the confessors could have prayed, fed, and affirmed the day; their account can no longer be amended.
The one who would not urge feeding the poor in 69:34 now has no food except a foul punitive food, an outcome shaped as a reversal of withheld nourishment.
The wicked are in Hell, supplying the debtor class whose entry into it on the Day of Recompense is stated in 82:15.
The righteous are in bliss, the favorable side of the same written account kept by the scribes in 82:10-12.
فَلَا صَدَّقَ وَلَا صَلَّىٰ joins failure to affirm with failure to pray, two liabilities the source and its Meʿārij parallel place in one account.
وَلَٰكِن كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ answers 75:31 with denial and turning away, making rejected truth the stance behind neglected worship.
The person “gave a little and then stopped,” a precise enactment of conceding only a minimal benefit before withholding even that.
Turning away introduces the person whose token giving and subsequent refusal are specified in 53:34.
The hypocrites forbid recognized good and close their hands, coupling social withholding with forgetfulness of God.
Believing men and women command recognized good, establish prayer, give zakāt, and obey God and His messenger, reversing each relevant count in 9:67 and the source scene.
Reform of the orphans' affairs is best; if property is mixed, they are brothers, and God knows the corrupter from the reformer, guarding the claimant behind the account.
When relatives, orphans, and needy people attend an estate division, they too must receive provision and kind speech, giving even the unassigned vulnerable attendee a share.
The fifth of spoils is assigned in part to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers, turning received wealth into specified social shares.
Fay is assigned to relatives, orphans, the needy, and travelers so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, the structural opposite of accumulated unpaid claims.
The ban on consuming one another's wealth falsely or using judges to take it knowingly protects the two-sided human account from legal manipulation.
Mutual wealth may not be consumed falsely but only exchanged through trade by consent, marking the boundary between a valid transaction and seizure of another's right.
A negotiated settlement between spouses is declared best while souls are prone to stinginess, placing reconciliation of rights directly against possessive withholding.
Tongues, hands, and feet testify to what people did on the day when God fully pays their true dīn in 24:25, supplying the evidence for that settlement.
Mouths are sealed while hands speak and feet testify to what was earned, preventing the liable party from denying the entries at audit.
The human being is informed that day of what was sent ahead and left behind, a concise statement of both sides of the personal record.
People will be questioned that day about enjoyed bounty, making received benefit itself an accountable entry rather than ownerless surplus.
All are returned to God, their true master; judgment belongs to Him and He is swiftest of reckoners, joining ownership, return, and account.
Each receives a share of what was earned and God is swift in account, stating both the booked portion and its prompt settlement.
After rejecting misappropriation by a prophet, the ayah says every soul will be paid in full for what it earned without wrong, linking entrusted property to final settlement.
“Is the recompense for excellence anything but excellence?” expresses jazāʾ as answering return, the repayment sense that the source places under dīn.
A wrong receives an equivalent recompense, while pardon and reconciliation earn a reward with God; exact balancing and merciful remission both belong within the account.
The givers who sought no human recompense in 76:9 are told that this is their recompense and their effort is thanked, transferring repayment to God.
إِنَّ ٱلدِّينَ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ ٱلْإِسْلَٰمُ explicitly identifies dīn with islām, confirming the source dictionary's underlying sense of submission.
A dīn other than islām will not be accepted and its seeker loses in the hereafter, joining submission now to the final balance.
God approves islām as dīn after completing the dīn and favor, again making dīn an accepted order of submission rather than only the future day.
Judgment belongs only to God, who commands worship of Him alone; ذَٰلِكَ ٱلدِّينُ ٱلْقَيِّمُ joins governing judgment and exclusive obedience in dīn.
Calling on God with dīn made sincere is followed by return as He first created people, binding exclusive obedience to the return for settlement.
Setting one's face to the upright dīn and God's created pattern presents dīn as the stable orientation of the whole person.
Turning repentantly to God, fearing Him, establishing prayer, and avoiding association unfolds the obedience required by the upright dīn of 30:30.
The covenant commands worship of God alone, kindness to orphans and the needy, prayer, and zakāt before charging most addressees with turning away, a near-complete ledger of the source's relations.
Prayer, zakāt, belief in God, and belief in the Last Day occur together and receive a great reward, joining present payment to confidence in the final account.
Guarding trusts and covenants continues the portrait of those who affirm the Day of Recompense, adding faithful discharge of two-party obligations to the Meʿārij reversal.
Wealth spent in God's way is multiplied like one seed yielding seven hundred, making a given amount a credit repaid far beyond its face value.
Satan promises poverty while God promises forgiveness and bounty, exposing the fear of loss that turns received good into withholding.
Concealed charity to the poor is better for the giver, supplying the opposite of a visible religious act detached from a true payment.
Those who spend by night and day, secretly and openly, have their wage with their Lord; continuous giving answers both withholding and concern for display.
Righteousness is not attained until people spend from what they love, opposing the attachment to wealth that erases another's share.
Mockers deride both generous voluntary donors and believers who can find only their own effort; the ayah protects the smallest sincere contribution from being treated as worthless.
God accepts repentance and takes charities, identifying the ultimate recipient and acknowledger of the payment made to human claimants.
Whatever people spend, God replaces it, and He is the best provider, answering fear that giving a benefit creates an unrepaid loss.
Charity is required before private consultation with the Messenger, making access carry a small payable social due before 58:13 mercifully waives it for those unable.
The question asks what harm would come from believing in God and the Last Day and spending from divine provision, directly reversing ostentatious spending without belief in 4:38.
The stingy denier is eased toward hardship, giving the consequence of the two linked counts in 92:8-9.
The most mindful person is kept away from the fire, introducing the giver whose motive is explained in 92:18-20.
The giver seeks only the face of the Most High Lord, locating recompense with God rather than in a human return.
The promise that the giver will be pleased closes the divine repayment of wealth given without a human debt.
كَتَبَ رَبُّكُمْ عَلَىٰ نَفْسِهِ ٱلرَّحْمَةَ pictures God as writing mercy upon Himself, a boundary showing that the owner of the account freely binds Himself to mercy.

The source's dictionary gloss of māʿūn as every benefit meets “what benefits people” remaining on earth here; the connection is indirect because this ayah contrasts enduring benefit with passing foam rather than alms.
The hand must be neither chained to the neck nor extended without limit, setting a measured boundary around the duty not to withhold.
The servants' spending is neither wasteful nor stingy but stands between them, clarifying that rejection of withholding does not erase proportion.
Fear of the Lord's punishment immediately follows affirmation of the Day of Recompense, supplying the accountable stance behind the passage's prayer and recognized wealth-right.
No soul receives delay when its term arrives, closing the deathbed wish in 63:10 to pay charity after the opportunity has ended.
Submitting one's face to God while doing good brings a wage with the Lord; this repeats the submission-and-recompense connection stated more explicitly elsewhere.
Whoever submits the face to God while doing good grasps the firm handhold, and the outcome of affairs is God's, linking yielded obedience to final disposition.
